title: The Worldly Traveler and the Wise Child
summary: A wealthy, worldly traveler who had spent his life in selfish indulgence and frivolous cynicism arrived at an inn in the suburbs of Baghdad. While sitting upon the veranda drink...
keywords: the debauchee and the three-year-old child
full_text:
A wealthy, worldly traveler who had spent his life in selfish indulgence and frivolous cynicism arrived at an inn in the suburbs of Baghdad. While sitting upon the veranda drinking sweet cordials and gloating over his business profits, he observed a three-year-old child who was playing with a small clay lamp upon the floor.

The child took a lighted wick, touched it to the lamp, and watched the flame burn brightly. Then, with a gentle breath, the child blew the flame out.

The cynical traveler, wishing to amuse himself by teasing the child with philosophical paradoxes, leaned forward with a mocking smile and asked: 'Tell me, little boy: where did the light go when you blew it out? If you can tell me where the flame has vanished, I will give you a bright gold dinar!'

The child looked at the traveler with clear, untroubled eyes, smiled with childlike simplicity, blew gently upon his empty fingertips, and asked:

'Tell me first, noble traveler: from whence did the light come before I ignited it? If you can tell me where the flame was hiding before the spark, I will give you my toy.'

The traveler stood frozen, struck dumb by the child’s profound, spontaneous answer. The mocking smile faded from his lips.

He looked at the tiny clay lamp, and realized with piercing clarity that all his worldly cynicism, clever sophistry, and accumulated wealth were powerless before the profound mysteries of existence and the purity of an innocent soul.

Tears of genuine humility welled in the traveler’s eyes. He put away his pride, distributed his gold to the poor of the inn, and devoted his remaining years to honest charity and philosophical study, having been awakened to truth by a three-year-old child.
moral: The innocent moral clarity of a child can awaken conscience faster than the sermons of philosophers.
